findings.where: Hero, the first-person paragraph under the headline ('I advise multilateral development banks…'), at desktop and phone
findings.fault: Mark's own first-person introduction is set in bold, widely letter-spaced capitals in the sans. It runs four lines on desktop and eight on phone, where 'PUBLIC-' is also hyphenated across a line break. A full sentence in tracked capitals is slow to read and looks like a label or a corporate banner, not a person speaking. The paragraph right below it is in the serif, in sentence case, so the two paragraphs of Mark's voice are set in two unrelated styles. The page's own type note says the sans is for 'notes and labels' and the serif is for Mark's voice, and this paragraph breaks that.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank officer reading the first screen would find the most important sentence about who Mark is the hardest one to read, and it comes across as a firm's tagline. The founder ruled that Mark must be heard in the first person and that nothing should read as a look any consultancy could own.

findings.where: Header, the name 'Mark M. Moseley' beside the mark and the nav
findings.fault: The name is set in a regular-weight serif at about 22 px, hardly larger than the semibold sans nav links across from it. The arches of the mark above 'MMM INFRA' are the heaviest thing in the header. As a result the name does not lead the lockup: it reads as a caption to the logo.
findings.who_objects: The founder's personal-advisor test says his name leads, with the logo beside it. A visitor scanning the header sees the firm's mark first and the person second.

findings.where: Email address: in the hero beside 'Write to me', and in the footer
findings.fault: The same address is set two ways. In the hero it is in the serif, in grey ink with a faint underline. In the footer it is in the sans, in the house blue with a solid underline. Next to the hero's sans buttons, the serif address looks like it belongs to a different system from the controls on either side of it.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who sees the address in two looks has no single cue for what is a contact detail. The founder asked for one direct way to reach Mark, and it should look the same wherever it appears.

findings.where: Article specimen, the photo caption ('A radio interview at the Belt and Road Summit. Placeholder: …'); also the hero portrait's caption
findings.fault: In the article, the italic serif caption and the small sans placeholder note run together on one line. The small text's second line ('the image round.') sits about a body line below, so the caption takes the 28 px body leading instead of its own tight setting. The hero portrait's caption stacks the same two parts as separate lines, so the same caption is set two ways on one page.
findings.who_objects: Angélique, who will publish captions on every article: the caption style is meant to show a rhythm that survives her content, and here the small caption text gets loose, body-sized gaps between its lines.

findings.where: Hero headline, desktop line 2 (‘perfect’ PPP Law – each)
findings.fault: The opening quotation mark sits inside the left text edge instead of hanging outside it. At this display size, the 'p' of 'perfect' looks visibly indented compared with the 'I', 'c' and 'i' that start the other lines.
findings.who_objects: A reader with an editorial eye, and the founder judging the first screen: the direction's premise is a well-set legal journal, and at 4rem the ragged-looking left edge reads as unfinished typesetting.
